toolCalls.output:
version: 2.1

parameters:
  setup_go:
    type: string
    default: github.com/circleci-functions/setup-go@v0.5.1-684fd5b

commands:
  setup:
    steps:
      - checkout
      - install-go
      - install-task

  # Installs the toolchain and restores the module, build and lint caches, saved at job end.
  install-go:
    steps:
      - run: circleci run << pipeline.parameters.setup_go >> --
          --version-file go.mod
          --golangci-lint-cache
          --checksum '{{ checksum "go.sum" }}_{{ checksum "clikit/go.sum" }}_{{ checksum "tools/go.sum" }}'
      - run: go version

  install-task:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Install go-task
          command: |
            sh -c "$(curl --location https://taskfile.dev/install.sh)" -- -d -b "$HOME/.local/bin"
            echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"

  # GoReleaser's dockers_v2 pipe shells out to `docker buildx build`, so the
  # builder and the registry login have to exist before it runs.
  setup-docker:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Register QEMU for cross-architecture builds
          # Dockerfile.alpine RUNs `apk add`, once per platform in the manifest,
          # so building its arm64 half on an amd64 host needs binfmt handlers
          # registered. Idempotent, and a no-op for the cimg/base image, which
          # only COPYs.
          command: docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64
      - run:
          name: Create a buildx builder
          # The machine image's default buildx driver is `docker`, which can
          # neither build for two platforms in one invocation nor push a
          # manifest list. A docker-container driver can do both.
          command: docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container
      - run:
          name: Log in to Docker Hub
          # Absent on branch dry-runs, which have no context: the snapshot build
          # still exercises the Dockerfile, it just pushes nothing.
          command: |
            if [ -z "${DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME:-}" ]; then
              echo "No Docker Hub credentials — skipping login (snapshot builds do not push)."
              exit 0
            fi
            echo "$DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD" | docker login --username "$DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME" --password-stdin

  store_results:
    steps:
      - store_test_results:
          path: ./test-reports

executors:
  linux:
    machine:
      image: ubuntu-2604:current
    resource_class: large.gen3

  # Arm64 counterpart to `linux`, for checking both halves of a multi-arch
  # image. Deliberately small: it only pulls and runs a container.
  linux-arm:
    machine:
      image: ubuntu-2604:current
    resource_class: arm.medium

  macos:
    macos:
      xcode: 26.5.0

  windows:
    machine: true
    resource_class: windows.medium

jobs:
  check:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:check
      - store_results

  test:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - setup
      - run: task ci:test
      - store_results

  mark-release:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Plan deployment
          command: |
            circleci run release plan "${CIRCLE_JOB}" \
              --environment-name="default" \
              --component-name="${CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME}" \
              --target-version="1.0.${CIRCLE_BUILD_NUM}-${CIRCLE_SHA1:0:7}"
      - run:
          name: Update deployment status to running
          command: circleci run release update "${CIRCLE_JOB}" --status=RUNNING
      - run:
          name: Update deployment status to success
          command: circleci run release update "${CIRCLE_JOB}" --status=SUCCESS
          when: on_success
      - run:
          name: Update deployment status to failed
          command: circleci run release update "${CIRCLE_JOB}" --status=FAILED
          when: on_fail

  deploy:
    executor: linux
    parameters:
      publish_steps:
        type: steps
        default:
          - run: task ci:release
    steps:
      - setup
      - setup-docker
      - run: sudo apt update --yes
      - run:
          name: Install snapcraft
          command: |
            sudo apt install snapd --yes
            sudo snap install snapcraft --classic
      - run:
          name: Install choco
          command: |
            sudo cp tools/choco.sh /usr/local/bin/choco
            sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/choco
            choco help
      - steps: << parameters.publish_steps >>
      - store_artifacts:
          path: dist

  smoke-test:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
      install-steps:
        type: steps
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - steps: << parameters.install-steps >>
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci binary
          command: circleci version

  # Matrixed over the executors rather than over the tags: only the architecture
  # needs a machine of its own, so each job checks both variants. Printing the
  # arch inside the container makes the log say which half of the manifest ran. A
  # tag missing this platform fails here anyway — the arm machine images carry no
  # binfmt, so there is nothing to silently emulate an amd64-only image with.
  smoke-test-docker:
    parameters:
      executor:
        type: executor
    executor: << parameters.executor >>
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci/circleci-cli:v1
          command: docker run --rm circleci/circleci-cli:v1 sh -c 'uname -m; circleci version'
      - run:
          name: Verify circleci/circleci-cli:v1-alpine
          command: docker run --rm circleci/circleci-cli:v1-alpine sh -c 'uname -m; circleci version'

  docs:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - run:
          name: Generate reference and build the site
          command: task docs:build
      - run:
          name: Check internal links
          command: task docs:test
      - store_artifacts:
          path: docs/website/public
      - persist_to_workspace:
          root: .
          paths:
            - "docs/website/public"

  docs-publish:
    executor: linux
    steps:
      - setup
      - attach_workspace:
          at: .
      - run:
          name: Publish to gh-pages
          command: task ci:docs:publish

  ok-to-deploy:
    type: no-op

workflows:
  ci:
    jobs:
      # gh-pages holds only generated HTML — never run CI on it. Entry jobs (no
      # `requires`) must opt out explicitly; downstream jobs are gated by these.

      - check:
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - test:
          matrix:
            parameters:
              executor:
                - linux
                - macos
                - windows
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - docs:
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore: gh-pages

      - deploy:
          name: dry-run
          publish_steps:
            - run: task ci:build
          filters:
            branches:
              ignore:
                - main
                - gh-pages

      - ok-to-deploy:
          requires:
            - check
            - test
            - docs
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - mark-release:
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy

      - deploy:
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/deploy
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release
            - macos-codesigning

      - docs-publish:
          serial-group: << pipeline.project.slug >>/docs-publish
          requires:
            - ok-to-deploy
          context:
            - devex-release

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-snap
          executor: linux
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install snapd
                command: sudo apt update --yes && sudo apt install snapd --yes
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Snap stable channel
                # /snap/bin has to be prepended, not just present: the machine
                # image ships its own circleci in /usr/local/bin, which would
                # otherwise shadow the snap and make this job verify the build
                # agent's CLI instead of the release.
                command: |
                  sudo snap install circleci
                  echo 'export PATH="/snap/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-brew
          executor: macos
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Homebrew preview tap
                command: |
                  brew update
                  rm -f /opt/homebrew/bin/circleci
                  brew install circleci-public/circleci/circleci@next
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test-docker:
          matrix:
            parameters:
              executor:
                - linux
                - linux-arm
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

      - smoke-test:
          name: smoke-test-choco
          executor: windows
          install-steps:
            - run:
                name: Install circleci via Chocolatey
                command: choco install circleci-cli -y
          requires:
            - deploy
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main

Get job details

## Usage

`circleci job get <job-id> [flags]`

## Arguments

`<job-id>` is the UUID of the job to look up. Job UUIDs are shown in
the output of `circleci workflow get` and `circleci run get --json`.

## Flags

| Flag          | Description                                                                       |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--jq string` | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`) |
| `--json`      | Output as JSON                                                                    |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- Get job details by UUID: 
  `circleci job get 8e50c384-0083-43d0-bc8f-93f0db589d6b`
- Output as JSON: 
  `circleci job get 8e50c384-0083-43d0-bc8f-93f0db589d6b --json`
- Get a specific field with jq: 
  `circleci job get 8e50c384-0083-43d0-bc8f-93f0db589d6b --json | jq '.status'`

## Details

Display the status and steps of a CircleCI job.

Job IDs are shown in the output of 'circleci workflow get' and
'circleci run get --json'.

JSON fields: id, name, type, status, started_at, stopped_at, project_id, pipeline_id, workflow_id, executions[].index/steps[].name/type/status/duration/exit_code

toolCalls.output:
Call the CircleCI REST API directly

## Usage

`circleci api <path> [flags]`

## Arguments

`<path>` is the request path. It is relative to /api/v3 by default
(for example, "projects/{project-id}"). To target
a different version prefix, include it explicitly, for example, "api/v2/me".

## Flags

| Flag                       | Description                                                                       |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-d, --data string`        | Raw request body sent verbatim; @file reads from a file, @- from stdin            |
| `-f, --field stringArray`  | Add a field: key=value (query param for GET/DELETE, JSON body for POST/PUT/PATCH) |
| `-H, --header stringArray` | Add a request header: "Key: Value"                                                |
| `--jq string`              | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`) |
| `-X, --method string`      | HTTP method (default: GET, or POST when -f or -d is used)                         |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- Get your user profile: 
  `circleci api me`
- List runs for a project: 
  `circleci api projects/{project-id}/runs`
- Trigger a pipeline on a branch: 
  `circleci api projects/{project-id}/run -f definition_id=<id> -f "config[branch]=main"`
- Send a body read from a file (@- reads from stdin): 
  `circleci api projects/{project-id}/run -d @payload.json`
- Access the v1.1 API with a custom header: 
  `circleci api api/v1.1/me -H "X-Custom: value"`

## Details

Make an authenticated HTTP request to the REST API and print the raw
response body. The Authorization header is added from your stored token.

Exit code reflects the HTTP response: 0 for 2xx, 4 for 4xx/5xx.
[exit code: 0]

List recent runs for a project

## Usage

`circleci run list [flags]`

Aliases: `circleci run ls`

## Flags

| Flag                   | Description                                                                       |

| `-b, --branch string`  | Filter by branch                                                                  |
| `-B, --current-branch` | Filter by the currently checked-out branch                                        |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- List recent runs for the current project: 
  `circleci run list`
- Filter to the branch you have checked out: 
  `circleci run list --current-branch`
- Filter to a specific branch: 
  `circleci run list --branch main`
- List runs for an explicit project: 
  `circleci run list --project gh/org/repo`
- Show more results: 
  `circleci run list --limit 25`
- Output as JSON for scripting: 
  `circleci run list --json`

## Details

List recent runs for a CircleCI project.

The project is inferred from the current git repository's remote
unless overridden with --project. Use --branch to filter results
to a single branch, or --current-branch (-B) to automatically use
the branch you have checked out.

The markdown table includes the commit subject; the JSON adds the full
commit and repository detail.

JSON fields: id, phase, outcome, current_outcome, branch, tag, revision, repository_url, commit.subject/url/author_name/author_login, created_at

List workflows for a run or recent runs

## Usage

`circleci workflow list [<run-id>] [flags]`

Aliases: `circleci workflow ls`

## Arguments

`<run-id>` is optional: a run UUID (as shown by `circleci run list --json`)
or a run number (as shown by `circleci run list`).

When omitted, workflows for recent runs in the current project are listed,
grouped by run.

## Flags

| Flag                  | Description                                                                       |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-b, --branch string` | Filter by branch (recent-runs mode)                                               |
| `--jq string`         | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`) |
| `--json`              | Output as JSON                                                                    |
| `--limit int`         | Number of recent runs to show (recent-runs mode) (default 10)                     |
| `--project string`    | Project slug (e.g. gh/org/repo); defaults to git remote                           |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- List workflows for recent runs in the current project: 
  `circleci workflow list`
- Filter to a specific branch: 
  `circleci workflow list --branch main`
- List workflows by run number: 
  `circleci workflow list 75`
- List workflows by run UUID: 
  `circleci workflow list 9e0c9d52-3b7e-4cd6-b5f7-bfc5e4a07e81`
- Output as JSON: 
  `circleci workflow list --json`

## Details

List workflows for a CircleCI run, or for recent runs in the project when
no run is given.

JSON fields (single run): id, name, phase, outcome, current_outcome.
Recent-runs mode adds run_id.

Get workflow details

## Usage

`circleci workflow get <workflow-id> [flags]`

## Arguments

`<workflow-id>` is the UUID of the workflow to look up. Workflow IDs are
shown in the output of `circleci run get`.

## Flags

| Flag          | Description                                                                       |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--jq string` | Process values from the response using jq syntax (see `circleci help formatting`) |
| `--json`      | Output as JSON                                                                    |

Global flags: `-c, --config`, `--debug`, `--no-color`, `-q, --quiet` — see `circleci --help`.

## Examples

- Get workflow details: 
  `circleci workflow get 5034460f-c7c4-4c43-9457-de07e2029e7b`
- Output as JSON: 
  `circleci workflow get 5034460f-c7c4-4c43-9457-de07e2029e7b --json`
- Get workflow ID from a run: 
  `circleci run get | grep -A1 "Workflows"`

## Details

Display the status and jobs of a CircleCI workflow.

Workflow IDs are shown in the output of 'circleci run get'.

JSON fields: id, name, phase, outcome, current_outcome, run_id, created_at, ended_at, jobs[].id/name/phase/outcome/current_outcome/type

I checked your `.circleci/config.yml` and looked at real job run data (via `circleci workflow`/`circleci job get`) to see how your resource classes line up with actual usage. A couple of caveats up front, then the findings.

**Limitation:** This environment doesn't let me query CircleCI's Insights/resource-usage API (`circleci api` is blocked here, and none of the other CLI commands expose CPU/RAM utilization). So I can't give you the same "X% CPU utilized" numbers you'd see on the CircleCI resource-class recommendation page. What I *can* do is compare declared resource classes against real job step timings from recent runs, which is a reasonable proxy.

**Resource classes declared:**
- `linux` executor → `machine` + `resource_class: large.gen3` — used by **check, test (linux), mark-release, deploy, docs, docs-publish, smoke-test-snap, smoke-test-docker (linux)**
- `linux-arm` → `machine` + `arm.medium`
- `windows` → `machine` + `windows.medium`
- `macos` → no `resource_class` set (uses the account's default `macos` size)

**What the actual run data shows:**

| Job | Real work time | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `mark-release` | **~2 seconds** (19:41:50 → 19:41:52) | 3 quick `circleci run release plan/update` API calls — no checkout, no build |
| `docs-publish` | ~36 seconds | attach workspace + `task ci:docs:publish` (git push to gh-pages) |
| `check` | ~1 min | full Go module/build/lint cache restore + `golangci-lint` |
| `docs` | ~40s | Go-based doc generation + link check |
| `test-linux` | ~1m40s | full Go test suite with `-race` |
| `deploy`/`dry-run` | ~2 min | docker buildx (cross-arch), snapcraft, choco installs, Go build |

`mark-release` stands out clearly: it does none of the heavy Go/Docker work the other jobs do, yet it's assigned the exact same `linux` executor (`large.gen3` machine) as the build/test/deploy jobs, and its actual work finishes in about 2 seconds. That's a strong case of a much larger resource class than the job needs — it would very likely run fine on a smaller machine size, or even a small Docker-executor image instead of a full machine VM.

`docs-publish` is a second, milder candidate: after the workspace is attached it just runs a git push task and finishes in well under a minute, so `large.gen3` is probably more than it needs too, though it does inherit Go/task tooling installation overhead from the shared `setup` command.

By contrast, `check`, `test-linux`, `docs`, and `deploy`/`dry-run` are doing real compute work (Go builds/tests with `-race`, linting, multi-arch Docker builds), so `large.gen3` is more defensible there — though only actual CPU/memory graphs (which I couldn't retrieve here) would confirm whether they're fully using it or could step down to `medium`.

**Bottom line:** Yes — `mark-release` (and to a lesser extent `docs-publish`) appear to be using a larger resource class (`large.gen3` machine) than their workload needs, since they reuse the same `linux` executor defined for your heavier build/test/deploy jobs. I'd suggest giving `mark-release` its own lightweight executor (e.g., a small Docker image, since it only makes CLI/API calls) rather than the shared machine executor. I did not make any changes to your config — this is just an assessment.
